# How to Write Better AI Prompts: A Practical Guide for Beginners

You've asked an AI to write an email, summarise a report, or plan your weekend — and the answer came back flat, weird, or just plain wrong. The AI isn't broken. The trick is in how you ask. A **prompt** (the instruction you type to an AI) is the difference between a useful answer and a wasted five minutes. Let's fix that.

## Why most prompts fall flat

Most people type something like *"write a social media post about my cafe"* and hope for magic. The AI has to guess: what tone? what platform? how long? what audience? When you leave all of that out, the AI fills the gaps with the most average answer it can think of.

Think of it like ordering coffee. "Coffee please" gets you a lukewarm default. "Large flat white, oat milk, extra hot, in a takeaway cup" gets you exactly what you want. The AI works the same way: the more specific you are, the better your result.

## Five techniques that work straight away

Here are five simple habits that turn mediocre outputs into genuinely useful ones. None of them require any technical knowledge.

**1. Tell the AI who it is, and who you're writing for.** Start with a role and an audience. For example: *"You are a friendly social media manager. Write a post for busy parents in their 30s."* This single sentence changes the tone completely.

**2. Show, don't just tell.** If you like a certain style, paste an example into your prompt and say *"write in a similar style"*. The AI will match the rhythm, length, and vibe. This is sometimes called **few-shot prompting** — basically, giving the AI a few examples to learn from.

**3. Specify the format you want.** Don't leave the structure to chance. Try ending your prompt with something like: *"Return the answer as a bulleted list"* or *"Keep it under 100 words"* or *"Give me three options to choose from"*. The AI follows these instructions far more reliably than you'd expect.

**4. Give the AI something to work with.** Instead of asking *"write me a cover letter"*, paste the job ad and your relevant experience into the prompt. The more raw material you provide, the more personalised the output. This applies to emails, recipes, study notes — anything.

**5. Iterate in the same chat.** If the first answer isn't quite right, don't start over. Reply with *"make it more friendly"* or *"shorter, please"* or *"add a question at the end"*. Each follow-up sharpens the result. The AI remembers the conversation, so you're building on previous attempts.

## A quick before-and-after

**Weak prompt:** *"Help me prepare for a job interview."*

**Better prompt:** *"I'm interviewing for a marketing coordinator role at a mid-sized company tomorrow. I've worked in retail for three years and have a Certificate IV in marketing. Give me five likely interview questions with short sample answers I can adapt. Keep the tone confident but not arrogant."*

Same AI. Same five minutes of your time. Wildly different result.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** Try the "role + audience + format" trick next time you ask an AI to help with a text message, a gift idea, or a recipe. You'll get something useful on the first try, not the third.
- **For your business or work:** Save your best prompts in a notes app. A good prompt for writing job ads, client emails, or social captions can be reused dozens of times with small tweaks. You'll get faster at it within a week.
- **If you're just getting started:** Pick one task you do every week — drafting a meeting recap, planning meals, summarising an article — and write a detailed prompt for it. Use it three times. Tweak it once. That's the whole skill.

## Wrap-up

Better prompting isn't about learning clever tricks or secret formulas. It's about being specific, giving examples, and telling the AI exactly what shape you want the answer in. Start with one prompt today: pick something real you need written, apply the five techniques above, and see what comes back. The difference will be obvious within a minute.
